lessons.title: Where Have the Fish Gone? Launching Our Investigation into Ecosystems

quiz.prompt: A learner sketches a river in Kenya to show what might be found in it. Which list has BOTH living and non-living things from a river?
choices: Tilapia, frogs, birds, insects
Tilapia, algae, water, sunlight
Water, oxygen, rocks, sand
Algae, aquatic weeds, tilapia, Nile perch
quiz.rationale: Tilapia and algae are living, while water and sunlight are non-living. The other lists contain only living things or only non-living things.
quiz.placement: Individual prediction and quick sketch showing living and non-living things in the river

quiz.prompt: A learner watched a video of a Kenyan river and filled in the 'What I see' column. Which entry is a specific observation rather than a general statement?
choices: Thick algae and aquatic weeds cover parts of the water
The river is in a bad state
The environment has been spoiled
People do not care about the river
quiz.rationale: Thick algae and weeds covering the water can be seen directly in the video. The other entries are opinions or general statements, not specific observations.
quiz.placement: Part A (Video): 3-column table 'What I see | What I hear | What I wonder'

quiz.prompt: In a river, all the tilapia living in the river together are called a:
choices: Community
Habitat
Population
Biome
quiz.rationale: A population is all the individuals of one species in an area, here all the tilapia in the river. A community includes many species together.
quiz.placement: Part B (Reading): table matching each term to an example from the river in the video

quiz.prompt: The river water and banks where the tilapia live is the tilapia's ___. The role the tilapia plays in the river, such as what it eats and how it lives, is its ___.
choices: community; population
niche; habitat
population; community
habitat; niche
quiz.rationale: A habitat is the place where an organism lives. A niche is the role of the organism in its ecosystem. Learners often confuse the two.
quiz.placement: Part B (Reading): group table matching habitat and niche to river examples

quiz.prompt: A group says, 'The fish are disappearing because they are old, or because they have no food.' They compare this idea with what was seen in the river video. Which is the best conclusion at this point?
choices: The idea should be ignored because it was only a prediction
The idea explains everything, so no more investigation is needed
The video has already proved the cause, so the question is solved
The idea explains only part of the evidence. The booming algae and weeds and the smell are still unexplained
quiz.rationale: Old age or lack of food does not account for the thick algae and weeds or the smell. These observations remain unexplained and need further investigation.
quiz.placement: Claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph comparing first ideas ('fish are old; fish have no food') with the video and reading

quiz.prompt: Learners are writing questions on sticky notes for the Driving Question Board about the river where fish are disappearing. Which question is the best one to investigate?
choices: Who owns the river?
Is the river dirty?
How do algae and weeds affect the fish in the river?
Are the fish old?
quiz.rationale: A good Driving Question Board question is open and can be investigated. The first two can be answered yes or no, and ownership does not help explain the ecosystem.
quiz.placement: Individual sticky-note questions and sorting into categories on the Driving Question Board

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is the best definition of an ecosystem?
choices: All the individuals of one species living in an area
The place where one organism lives
The living things in an area together with the non-living parts of their environment, interacting with each other
All the non-living things in an area, such as water, light and temperature
quiz.rationale: An ecosystem includes both living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components that interact in an area. The other choices describe a population, a habitat and abiotic factors only.
quiz.placement: Exit Ticket (1): Define ecosystem in your own words

lessons.title: Who Lives Where? Habitat Classification and Adaptations in a Kenyan River and Beyond

quiz.prompt: Mangrove trees grow in the salty mud at Mida Creek near Mombasa. Which habitat group do mangroves belong to?
choices: Xerophytes
Mesophytes
Halophytes
Hydrophytes
quiz.rationale: Mangroves live in salty conditions, so they are halophytes. Learners may say hydrophyte because mangroves stand in water, but the key habitat condition is salt.
quiz.placement: Predict: six quick prompts on the board (mangrove at Mombasa, Mida Creek)

quiz.prompt: Euphorbia in dry Turkana has a thick, fleshy stem covered with a waxy layer. How does this waxy layer help it survive?
choices: It removes extra salt from the plant
It helps the plant take in dissolved oxygen
It reduces the amount of water lost from the plant
It helps the plant float on water
quiz.rationale: Euphorbia is a xerophyte. A thick waxy cuticle reduces water loss, which is vital in a dry habitat.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Round 1: expert group on xerophytes (Euphorbia, sisal, Opuntia, acacia)

quiz.prompt: Water hyacinth on Lake Victoria has leaves with large air spaces inside. What is the main use of these air spaces?
choices: They help the leaves float at the water surface
They store water for the dry season
They let the plant lose water quickly in hot weather
They let the plant breathe through gills
quiz.rationale: Water hyacinth is a hydrophyte. Air spaces in its leaves and stems make it buoyant, so it floats and gets light at the surface.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Round 1: expert group on hydrophytes (water hyacinth, water lily, papyrus)

quiz.prompt: Why can a tilapia not live in a desert?
choices: It cannot grow thick fur for the cold desert nights
It has a hump that stores too much water
Desert air has too much oxygen for it
Its gills only work in water, where they take in dissolved oxygen
quiz.rationale: Aquatic animals such as tilapia use gills to get dissolved oxygen from water. Without water they cannot get oxygen, so they cannot survive in a desert.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Round 2: oral question 'Why can a tilapia not live in a desert?'

quiz.prompt: A Kenyan river once had many fish, but now has much algae and many weeds and sometimes smells bad. Which explanation best fits what the class learned about habitats and adaptations?
choices: Algae and weeds are xerophytes, so they grow best when the river dries up
The fish are old and the algae grow because the fish have stopped eating them
The fish have no food, so the algae and weeds have taken over the river
Nutrient-rich, warm water favours algae and weeds. When they die and decay, they use up dissolved oxygen, which harms fish that breathe with gills
quiz.rationale: Hydrophytes and algae thrive in nutrient-rich water. Their decay lowers dissolved oxygen and causes smell, and fish depend on that oxygen. The other options repeat the learners' first ideas or misname the plants.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Round 2: claim-evidence-reasoning on why algae and aquatic weeds grow well while fish decline

quiz.prompt: A camel in Marsabit has a hump and can go for long periods without drinking. How did camels come to have these adaptations?
choices: The desert heat changes the body of every young camel into a desert type
Camels with helpful features survived and passed them on over many generations
Camels chose to develop a hump when they entered the desert
Each camel grew a hump during its life because it needed water
quiz.rationale: Adaptations are not chosen by the organism. They arise over generations through natural selection, as individuals with useful features survive and reproduce.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Round 2: teacher addresses the misconception about how adaptations arise (camel, desert animals)

quiz.prompt: In a model of the river, a learner draws the arrow 'Nutrients → algae → less oxygen → fish?' and puts a question mark at the end. Why is the question mark used?
choices: Because fish do not need oxygen
Because this is only a possible link until there is evidence to support it
Because the arrows must always end with a question mark
Because algae are not found in rivers
quiz.rationale: The arrow is a possible link between nutrients, algae, oxygen and fish. The question mark shows it is still an idea to be tested with evidence in later lessons.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the river ecosystem sketch with the example arrow 'Nutrients → algae → less oxygen → fish?'

lessons.title: Counting Life: Characteristics of Populations and Direct Counting in the School Compound

quiz.prompt: Villagers beside a Kenyan river say, "There used to be many fish." Which action would best turn this statement into evidence?
choices: Look at the river and guess how many fish are there
Count the fish in a known area at different times and compare the numbers
Ask more villagers whether they agree
Wait to see if the smell of the water goes away
quiz.rationale: Evidence comes from measurement. Counting individuals in a known area at different times lets us compare numbers, whereas opinions and guesses are not reliable.
quiz.placement: Predict: recall the river video and write a prediction (fact or opinion, how to turn it into evidence)

quiz.prompt: What do we call all the fish of one species living together in the same river?
choices: A community
A habitat
An ecosystem
A population
quiz.rationale: A population is all the individuals of one species living in the same place at the same time. A community includes all the species, and a habitat is the place where they live.
quiz.placement: Predict: introducing the word 'population' (What do we call all the fish of one species in the river?)

quiz.prompt: A group marks a 10 m x 10 m area on the school field and counts 250 grass tufts. What is the population density of grass tufts?
choices: 25 per m²
2.5 per m²
0.4 per m²
350 per m²
quiz.rationale: Area = 10 m x 10 m = 100 m². Density = number of individuals / area = 250 / 100 = 2.5 per m².
quiz.placement: Observe: jigsaw counting at Site A and Site B, Calculator finds density

quiz.prompt: During the jigsaw counting, why must the group agree on what counts as ONE plant before they start counting?
choices: So that the density will always be a whole number
So that everyone counts in the same way and no plant is counted twice or missed
So that the counting finishes faster
So that the area marked will be larger
quiz.rationale: A clear counting rule keeps the count consistent and honest. It avoids double counting and missed plants, which would make the data unreliable.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher demonstration of marking the 10 m x 10 m area and agreeing on what counts as ONE plant

quiz.prompt: Site A has 300 weeds in a 10 m x 10 m area. Site B has 300 weeds in a 20 m x 10 m area. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both sites have the same density because they have the same number of weeds
Site B has the higher density because its area is larger
Site A has the higher density because the same number of weeds is found in a smaller area
Density cannot be compared unless the number of weeds is different
quiz.rationale: Site A density = 300 / 100 = 3 per m². Site B density = 300 / 200 = 1.5 per m². The same number in a smaller area means a higher density, so number alone does not show density.
quiz.placement: Explain: difference between population size and population density, and correcting the misconception that more individuals always means higher density

quiz.prompt: Which situation is suitable for the direct counting method?
choices: Counting the trees growing in a small school plot
Counting the insects flying over a whole forest
Counting all the fish in Lake Victoria
Counting all the algae cells in a river
quiz.rationale: Direct counting suits small populations whose individuals are easy to see, identify and count, such as trees in a small plot. Fish, algae and flying insects are too many, hidden or mobile.
quiz.placement: Explain: when direct counting is suitable and whether it would work for fish or algae in a river

quiz.prompt: Why would direct counting of every fish in a river be difficult?
choices: Rivers have no area that can be measured
Fish do not belong to any population
Fish density cannot be calculated using area
Fish can move and hide in deep water, so they cannot all be seen and counted
quiz.rationale: Fish swim, hide and are hidden in deep water, so counting every individual is not possible. Other methods, such as sampling, are needed.
quiz.placement: Explain: probing the river link (If fish swim, hide in deep water and cannot be seen, can we count every one?)

quiz.prompt: A group counted grass in two 10 m x 10 m areas of the school field. A learner asks, "Do these two counts tell us how the grass is spread over the whole field?" What is the best answer?
choices: Not necessarily, because two small areas may not represent the whole field, so we need to test if the distribution is uniform
No, because density is not affected by where the area is
Yes, because any two areas will always show the whole field
Yes, because direct counting always works for the whole field
quiz.rationale: Two small areas give information only about those places. Conditions such as shade, soil and trampling can vary, so we must investigate whether the grass is spread evenly across the field.
quiz.placement: DQB: update the board and ask 'Did our two 10 m x 10 m areas tell us about the whole field?'

quiz.prompt: A site has 180 plants in a 100 m² area. What is the population density?
choices: 0.18 per m²
18 per m²
1.8 per m²
80 per m²
quiz.rationale: Population density = number of individuals / area = 180 / 100 = 1.8 per m².
quiz.placement: Model: exit ticket question 2 (density for 180 plants in 100 m²)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly defines population density?
choices: The total number of species in an ecosystem
The number of individuals counted in the whole habitat
The number of individuals of a species per unit area
The area occupied by one individual of a species only
quiz.rationale: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area, calculated as number of individuals divided by area sampled.
quiz.placement: Model: exit ticket question 1 (Define population density)

lessons.title: Quadrat Sampling: Is the Distribution of Grass and Weeds Uniform Across the School Field?

quiz.prompt: A team is sampling the grass and weeds in a zone of the school field using a 1 m x 1 m quadrat. Why must they place the quadrat at random locations instead of where the grass looks nicest?
choices: So that every quadrat contains exactly the same number of plants
So that the sample is not biased and represents the whole zone
So that the counting is finished faster
So that only the most common weed is counted
quiz.rationale: Random placement removes bias, so the small sampled area fairly represents the whole zone. Choosing spots by eye would over- or under-estimate the population.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 1 (expert groups): placing the quadrat at 5 random locations in their zone

quiz.prompt: A team places a 1 m x 1 m quadrat at 5 random spots in a sunny zone of the school field. The numbers of weed plants counted are 12, 8, 10, 15 and 5. What is the density of weeds in plants per m²?
choices: 10 plants per m²
5 plants per m²
15 plants per m²
50 plants per m²
quiz.rationale: Total counted = 12 + 8 + 10 + 15 + 5 = 50. Density = 50 plants / (5 quadrats x 1 m²) = 10 plants per m².
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 1 (expert groups): calculating total counted, mean per quadrat and density

quiz.prompt: In a damp zone of the school field, the mean number of grass tufts is 6 per 1 m x 1 m quadrat. The zone has a total area of 200 m². What is the estimated total number of grass tufts in the zone?
choices: 33 tufts
1200 tufts
120 tufts
206 tufts
quiz.rationale: Density = 6 tufts per m². Estimated population = density x total area = 6 x 200 = 1200 tufts.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 1 (expert groups): estimated population = density x total area of the zone

quiz.prompt: A class uses quadrats to estimate that there are 1200 weed plants in a zone. Why is this number only an estimate?
choices: Weeds cannot be counted accurately because they are too small
Quadrats can only be used on grass and not on weeds
The area of the quadrat was not known
Only a small part of the zone was sampled and the result is assumed to represent the whole zone
quiz.rationale: Quadrat sampling counts a small part of the habitat and scales it up. Chance and the number of quadrats used mean the true total may differ.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 2 (home groups): question 3 on how the quadrat method gives an estimate and why it is only an estimate

quiz.prompt: Home groups compare the mean plant density of two zones on the school field: 42 plants per m² in a damp zone near a tap and 6 plants per m² in a heavily trampled zone. Which claim is best supported by this evidence?
choices: Trampling has been proved to be the only cause of the low density
The distribution of plants is not uniform, because density was much higher in the damp zone than in the trampled zone
The damp zone is healthier because more plants always means a healthier ecosystem
The distribution of plants is uniform, because plants grow everywhere on the field
quiz.rationale: The numbers show a clear difference in density between zones, so plants are not evenly spread. The data show a pattern but do not prove a single cause, and more plants does not always mean a healthier ecosystem.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 2 (home groups): claim-evidence-reasoning statement on chart paper

quiz.prompt: Along a Kenyan river, aquatic weeds and algae grow thickly in one stretch where fertiliser and sewage from nearby farms enter the water. Fish are fewer there. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Fish are fewer only because they are old and have no food
Extra nutrients let algae and weeds boom, which can reduce oxygen in the water and harm the fish
More weeds means more food and oxygen, so the fish there are healthier
The weeds grow thickly only because the water is the same everywhere along the river
quiz.rationale: Nutrient enrichment causes algae and weeds to boom. This can lower oxygen levels and harm fish, so more plants is not always a sign of a healthy ecosystem.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw Step 2 (home groups): question 4 linking weeds and algae in the river to the field patterns

quiz.prompt: On the school field, plant density is much lower on a heavily used footpath than beside a tap. Which is the best explanation?
choices: Trampling and compacted soil damage plants and limit root growth, while the soil beside the tap has more water
Plants need no water, so the tap makes no difference to density
Seeds cannot grow anywhere that the soil is wet
Plants are spread evenly, so the difference must be due only to counting mistakes
quiz.rationale: Environmental conditions such as trampling, soil compaction and water availability affect plant populations. Plants are not spread evenly, and these factors can explain the difference in density.
quiz.placement: Exit ticket: prompt 2 on two reasons why plant density may differ between two parts of a habitat

lessons.title: Belt Transect Across a Changing Habitat: How Does Plant Population Change as Conditions Change?

quiz.prompt: Before collecting data, a learner predicts that a shaded area of the school compound will have fewer grass plants per square metre than the open field. Which reason best supports this prediction?
choices: Plants in the shade do not need any water
Grass grows best when it gets no sunlight at all
Shade gives less sunlight, so the grass can make less food by photosynthesis
Shaded areas always have more trampling than open fields
quiz.rationale: Light is an abiotic factor that limits plant growth. Less light means less photosynthesis, so fewer plants are expected in the shade.
quiz.placement: Predict: sketching a prediction of plant abundance across the four zones and writing one sentence explaining why

quiz.prompt: In a belt transect study, a group places quadrats at regular intervals (every 2 m) between two parallel lines instead of choosing the greenest spots. Why is this done?
choices: It avoids bias, so the sample represents the whole transect and not only the best places
It makes sure every quadrat contains the same number of plants
It protects the plants from being trampled by the learners
It makes the counting finish faster because there are fewer plants to count
quiz.rationale: Regular spacing removes personal choice. This gives a fair picture of how plant numbers change along the whole transect.
quiz.placement: Observe: laying out the belt transect and placing quadrats every 2 m between the two lines

quiz.prompt: Team A counted the plants in five 1 m x 1 m quadrats placed in the open field: 16, 20, 18, 22 and 14 plants. What is the mean abundance per quadrat in the open field?
choices: 22 plants
18 plants
90 plants
20 plants
quiz.rationale: Mean = total plants ÷ number of quadrats = (16 + 20 + 18 + 22 + 14) ÷ 5 = 90 ÷ 5 = 18 plants per quadrat.
quiz.placement: Explain: calculating the mean abundance for each zone in home groups

quiz.prompt: A group uses a 50 cm x 50 cm quadrat (area 0.25 m²) in the garden zone. The mean count is 3 plants per quadrat. What is the estimated density in plants per square metre?
choices: 0.75 plants per m²
6 plants per m²
12 plants per m²
3 plants per m²
quiz.rationale: Density = mean count ÷ area of quadrat = 3 ÷ 0.25 = 12 plants per m². Four of these small quadrats make 1 m².
quiz.placement: Explain: estimating density (plants per square metre) from the quadrat data

quiz.prompt: The school pathway gets plenty of sunlight, but the transect showed very few plants growing on it. What is the best explanation?
choices: Plants on pathways have no competition, so they cannot grow
Too much sunlight kills all plants
Constant trampling damages plants and compacts the soil, so few plants can grow
Pathways have no soil at all
quiz.rationale: Trampling is a limiting factor. It crushes plants and compacts the soil even where light is plentiful.
quiz.placement: Explain: writing a claim-evidence-reasoning explanation using the light, moisture and trampling data

quiz.prompt: In the school garden, manure and water were added and weeds grew very thickly. A river near a farm receives fertiliser and sewage, and algae and aquatic weeds grow thickly there too. Which statement best links the two situations?
choices: Fish eat the algae, so the algae are the cause of the fish disappearing
Extra nutrients boost the growth of plants and algae in both places, as the manure does in the garden
Extra nutrients reduce the growth of algae in rivers but increase it in gardens
Algae and weeds in the river are many, so the river must be healthier now
quiz.rationale: Added nutrients (manure or fertiliser and sewage) remove a limit on growth, so plants or algae increase. More plants does not always mean a healthier habitat.
quiz.placement: Explain: comparing school compound factors with river factors (nutrients from farms and sewage)

quiz.prompt: Which pair of factors that could affect fish in a river contains one abiotic factor and one biotic factor?
choices: Oxygen level in the water and competition for food among fish
Algae and aquatic weeds
Water temperature and nutrient level
Sunlight and water temperature
quiz.rationale: Oxygen level is a non-living (abiotic) factor, and competition for food between living organisms is a biotic factor. The other pairs are both abiotic or both biotic.
quiz.placement: Model: adding abiotic and biotic factors affecting algae, weeds and fish to the river model

quiz.prompt: In the shaded part of the school compound, few plants grew because there was little light. In ecology, what do we call a condition like this that restricts how large a population can grow?
choices: A quadrat
A limiting factor
A habitat
A niche
quiz.rationale: A limiting factor, such as light, nutrients, space or trampling, restricts population size. A niche is the role of an organism, a habitat is where it lives, and a quadrat is a sampling frame.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: exit ticket on factors affecting plant population size

lessons.title: How Many Fish Are Left? Capture-Recapture Simulation to Estimate Population Size

quiz.prompt: Fishers say there are fewer fish in a Kenyan river, but the fish are hidden under the water and keep moving. Why do scientists use a sampling method such as capture-recapture instead of counting every fish?
choices: Fishers are not allowed to count fish
Sampling gives the exact number of fish, but counting does not
Counting every moving fish in a river is not practical, so a sample is used to estimate the total
Fish are too small to be counted by people
quiz.rationale: Mobile organisms hidden in water cannot be counted one by one, so a marked sample is used to estimate the population. The result is an estimate, not an exact count.
quiz.placement: Predict: individual prediction and think-pair-share on how to find out how many fish are in the river

quiz.prompt: In a capture-recapture simulation, 15 counters are captured and marked, then returned and mixed. A second sample of 20 counters is taken and 5 of them are marked. What is the estimated population?
quiz.rationale: Estimate = (number marked x number in second sample) / number of marked recaptured = (15 x 20) / 5 = 300 / 5 = 60.
quiz.placement: Observe: capture-recapture simulation with 100 counters (Recorder/Calculator role)

quiz.prompt: In the simulation, a group forgets to mix the marked counters thoroughly with the others before taking the second sample. Why is this a problem?
choices: The second sample may not represent the whole population, so the estimate can be badly wrong
The container would hold more than 100 counters
The marked counters would change colour
The formula would no longer have a number for the marked counters
quiz.rationale: The method assumes the marked individuals are fully mixed. If they are not, the second sample is not a fair sample of the population and the estimate becomes unreliable.
quiz.placement: Observe: Recapturer mixes and takes the second random sample

quiz.prompt: Fisheries officers on Lake Victoria catch and tag 50 Nile tilapia and release them. Later they catch 60 fish, and 12 of them have tags. What is the estimated number of tilapia in the lake?
quiz.placement: Explain: Lake Victoria problem comparing the second year (50 tagged, 60 caught, 12 tagged)

quiz.prompt: Fisheries officers tag 40 fish in a lake. In Year A, they catch 50 fish and 5 are tagged. In Year B, they again catch 50 fish and 10 are tagged. What does this suggest about the fish population in Year B compared with Year A?
choices: It is the same, because the same number of fish were tagged and caught
It cannot be compared, because the estimates are not numbers
It is smaller, because a larger share of the catch is tagged
It is larger, because more tagged fish were found
quiz.rationale: Year A estimate = (40 x 50) / 5 = 400. Year B estimate = (40 x 50) / 10 = 200. More tagged fish recaptured means the marked fish make up a larger share of the population, so the population is smaller.
quiz.placement: Explain: discussion of what happens to the estimate if more or fewer marked individuals are recaptured

quiz.prompt: During a capture-recapture study, many of the tags fall off the tagged fish before the second catch. How will this affect the estimated population size?
choices: There will be no effect, because the formula uses only the second sample
The estimate will be too large, because fewer tagged fish are recognised in the second catch
The estimate will be exact, because tags do not matter
The estimate will be too small, because fewer fish are counted
quiz.rationale: If tags are lost, fewer marked fish are recaptured. Since the number recaptured is in the denominator, the estimate becomes larger than the true population.
quiz.placement: Explain: listing the assumptions of the method (marks are not lost) and how they might be broken

quiz.prompt: A class uses capture-recapture on a river and gets an estimate of 500 fish in one year and 250 fish in the next year. Which conclusion is best supported by this evidence?
choices: The estimates suggest the fish population has fallen, but more investigation is needed to find the cause
The estimates prove that overfishing is the cause of the decline
The estimates are exact counts, so exactly 250 fish died
The estimates prove that pollution is the cause of the decline
quiz.rationale: The method estimates numbers and shows a likely decline, but it does not explain why the numbers dropped. Causes such as pollution or overfishing need further evidence.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the class river model with an arrow and a question mark for the causes of the decline (500 to 250)

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Population Size: Why Are the Fish Disappearing?

quiz.prompt: Learners sorted factors that could reduce fish numbers in a Kenyan river into 'living' and 'non-living'. Which choice correctly gives one biotic factor and one abiotic factor?
choices: Biotic: water temperature; abiotic: disease and parasites
Biotic: drought lowering water level; abiotic: algae cover
Biotic: dissolved oxygen; abiotic: competition among tilapia
Biotic: Nile perch preying on small fish; abiotic: low dissolved oxygen in the water
quiz.rationale: Predation by Nile perch involves living organisms, so it is biotic. Dissolved oxygen is a non-living part of the environment, so it is abiotic. The other choices swap the two categories.
quiz.placement: Predict: pair-share and sort ideas into 'living things' and 'non-living things'

quiz.prompt: After reading about population growth and limiting factors, which statement best describes the carrying capacity of a river for tilapia?
choices: The maximum number of tilapia that the river's resources can support over time
The number of tilapia that fishermen are allowed to catch each season
The number of tilapia born in the river each year
The number of different fish species living in the river
quiz.rationale: Carrying capacity is the maximum population size an environment can support, given food, space, oxygen and other resources. It is not a birth rate, a fishing quota or a count of species.
quiz.placement: Part A: Khan Academy reading on population growth and limiting factors (meaning of carrying capacity)

quiz.prompt: In a simulation, a group first runs a baseline with fish and food only. In trial 2 they add predators and change nothing else. The fish population ends lower than in the baseline. Why can they conclude that predators caused the drop?
choices: Because the graph in trial 2 has more lines than the graph in the baseline
Because predators are always the most important factor in any ecosystem
Because only one variable was changed, so the predators are the only difference between the trials
Because the fish population was lower at the start of trial 2
quiz.rationale: When only one variable is changed per trial, any difference in the results can be linked to that variable. This is why learners were told to change only ONE thing at a time.
quiz.placement: Part B: PhET simulation, trial 2 (adding predators) with one variable changed at a time

quiz.prompt: In the PhET simulation, learners keep the fish but reduce the amount of food available. What do they most likely observe on the fish population graph?
choices: The fish population stops growing and falls to a lower level, because food is a limiting factor
The fish population rises quickly, then the food increases
The fish population keeps rising because there are no predators
The fish population stays exactly the same as the baseline
quiz.rationale: Food availability limits how many fish can survive. With less food the environment supports fewer fish, so the population is lower than in the baseline.
quiz.placement: Part B: PhET simulation, trial 3 (reducing food)

quiz.prompt: A river receives fertiliser and sewage from farms and homes upstream. Fish numbers fall while algae and weeds increase and the water smells bad. Which explanation best links these observations?
choices: Excess nutrients cause an algae boom. When the algae die and decompose, dissolved oxygen falls and fish cannot survive.
Algae cover lets more light reach the bottom of the river, which makes the fish leave.
Algae are poisonous, so they kill the fish directly as soon as they appear.
Extra nutrients give the fish more food, so the fish grow old and die in large numbers.
quiz.rationale: Nutrients feed algae, which then die and decompose. Decomposition uses up dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate. Algae cover also reduces light, so it does not increase it.
quiz.placement: Discussion Diamond: ranking the nine factor cards and claim-evidence-reasoning response 'Why are fish disappearing while algae increase?'

quiz.prompt: Tilapia in a dam breed every few months, yet their population stops increasing at about 5 000 fish and stays near that number. What is the best explanation?
choices: The tilapia choose to stop breeding when the dam looks full
Limiting factors such as food, oxygen and space prevent the population from growing beyond what the dam can support
Population size can only grow until it reaches 5 000 in any water body
Predators are the only factor that can control a population
quiz.rationale: Limiting factors (food, dissolved oxygen, space, predation, disease) set the carrying capacity, so no population can grow forever. More than one factor usually acts together, so predators are not the only control.
quiz.placement: Discussion Diamond: oral question 'Why can a population not grow forever?'

quiz.prompt: Learners are adding human activities to their river ecosystem model and linking them to nutrient input. Which human activity should they connect to extra nutrients in the water?
choices: Nile perch preying on small fish
Drought lowering the water level
Tilapia competing for food
Fertiliser from farms and untreated sewage washing into the river
quiz.rationale: Fertiliser runoff and untreated sewage are human activities that add nitrogen and other nutrients to water. Predation, drought and competition are natural factors and do not add nutrients.
quiz.placement: Revising the ecosystem model of the river: adding human activity (fishing, fertiliser from farms, untreated sewage)

lessons.title: Nitrogen and Carbon Cycles: How Nutrients Move and Why Algae Boom in Our River

quiz.prompt: Farmers in Kisii and Bungoma often plant beans between rows of maize. Which process in the bean roots helps the maize crop get more nitrogen?
choices: Bean roots take in nitrogen gas and release it directly to the maize roots
Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules change nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds
Denitrifying bacteria in the soil change nitrates into nitrogen gas for the maize
Bean leaves use photosynthesis to make nitrates for the maize
quiz.rationale: Rhizobium bacteria in bean and groundnut root nodules fix nitrogen gas into compounds that plants can use, and the soil is enriched with them. Denitrification removes usable nitrogen, so it does not help.
quiz.placement: Guided discussion: 'Why do farmers in Kisii and Bungoma plant beans between maize rows?'

quiz.prompt: A student says, 'Maize plants take nitrogen gas straight from the air and use it to make proteins.' Which is the best correction?
choices: Maize can only get nitrogen by eating dead animals
Maize gets nitrogen from carbon dioxide during photosynthesis
Maize absorbs nitrates from the soil, which were made by nitrogen fixation and nitrification
Maize absorbs nitrogen gas through its stomata, but only at night
quiz.rationale: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly. They absorb nitrates through their roots, and these come from fixation (bacteria, lightning) and nitrification of ammonium.
quiz.placement: Cycle cards: nitrogen fixation, nitrification, nitrates absorbed by maize and sukuma wiki

quiz.prompt: A dairy cow in Kericho dies and its body decays in the soil. Which organisms release the nitrogen from its proteins as ammonium so that it can re-enter the nitrogen cycle?
choices: Producers such as maize
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in bean roots only
Consumers such as other cattle
Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi
quiz.rationale: Decomposers break down dead organisms and release nitrogen as ammonium, which nitrifying bacteria then change to nitrates. Producers and consumers do not do this breakdown.
quiz.placement: Circulating question: 'What happens to the nitrogen when the cow dies?'

quiz.prompt: A learner eats ugali and then runs. Which process returns carbon from the ugali to the air as carbon dioxide?
choices: Denitrification in the learner's muscles
Nitrification in the learner's stomach
Photosynthesis in the learner's cells
Respiration in the body's cells
quiz.rationale: Cells use respiration to release energy from food, and carbon dioxide is given off and breathed out. Photosynthesis takes CO2 in and happens in plants, not animals.
quiz.placement: Guided discussion: 'Where does the carbon in your ugali end up when you run?'

quiz.prompt: Which list contains only processes that return carbon dioxide to the air in the carbon cycle?
choices: Photosynthesis, burning charcoal and nitrification
Nitrogen fixation, respiration and burning firewood
Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition
Respiration, decomposition and burning firewood
quiz.rationale: Respiration, decomposition (microbial respiration) and combustion of firewood or fossil fuels all release CO2. Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the air.
quiz.placement: Cycle cards for carbon: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion of firewood and fossil fuels

quiz.prompt: Rain washes fertiliser from maize farms, cattle waste and sewage into a river. Why does this make algae and water weeds grow very fast?
choices: The fertiliser makes the water colder, so the algae grow faster
The sewage gives the algae more oxygen to breathe
The water gains extra nitrates and phosphates that the algae and weeds use to grow
The algae feed directly on the fish in the river
quiz.rationale: Fertiliser, manure and sewage add nitrates and phosphates (nutrient enrichment), which allow algae and weeds to multiply quickly.
quiz.placement: Groups' 4-5 sentence explanation: how too much nitrates and phosphates lead to more algae

quiz.prompt: In a river with an algal bloom, the algae and weeds die in large numbers. Why do fish then die?
choices: The fish die of old age because the water is warmer
The fish have no food because algae are the only food in rivers
Decomposing bacteria multiply and use up dissolved oxygen, so the fish cannot get enough
The dead algae release extra oxygen that is poisonous to fish
quiz.rationale: Dead algae and weeds feed decomposers, which use dissolved oxygen in respiration. Low oxygen causes fish to suffocate, which corrects the idea that fish simply have no food.
quiz.placement: Chain scaffold: 'If decomposers use oxygen, what happens to fish that need oxygen?'

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct order of events in the river after fertiliser and sewage runoff enter it?
choices: Decomposers use up oxygen, nutrient enrichment, algae and weeds die, algal bloom, fish die
Algal bloom, nutrient enrichment, fish die, decomposers use up oxygen, algae and weeds die
Fish die, decomposers use up oxygen, nutrient enrichment, algal bloom, algae and weeds die
Nutrient enrichment, algal bloom, algae and weeds die, decomposers use up oxygen, fish die
quiz.rationale: Enrichment comes first and causes the bloom. The bloom dies and is decomposed, oxygen is used up, and fish suffocate.
quiz.placement: Groups sequence the chain: runoff, nutrient enrichment, algal bloom, ... fish suffocate

quiz.prompt: Along a polluted river, people notice a foul smell after many algae and weeds have died. What is the best explanation?
choices: The smell comes from nitrogen gas escaping from the water
With little oxygen left, anaerobic decay of the dead matter produces foul-smelling substances
Fish release a bad smell when they are hungry
Algae produce a bad smell only when they are alive and healthy
quiz.rationale: When oxygen is used up, decay continues without oxygen (anaerobic decay) and produces foul-smelling products.
quiz.placement: Chain: anaerobic decay produces foul smell (explanation writing)

quiz.prompt: A student hears a group claim 'the fish are disappearing because they have no food.' What evidence from the river would best show this claim is incomplete?
choices: The river still has some fish in it
The river is flowing towards Lake Victoria
Algae and weeds are growing fast while dissolved oxygen falls after they die and decompose
Beans are planted near the river
quiz.rationale: Plenty of algae and weeds means food is not the only problem. Oxygen loss from decomposition explains the fish loss, which is the point to note when learners say fish have no food.
quiz.placement: Peer review and revision: noting learners who still say 'fish have no food' without mentioning oxygen

lessons.title: Pollution, Garbage Rivers and Restoring Our River: The Final Explanation

quiz.prompt: Before a walk to the shopping centre, learners predict where the water from drains goes when it rains. Which statement best describes the likely pathway of pollutants such as oil, soapy water and litter from a shopping centre?
choices: They are washed by rain into drains and carried to a nearby river
They evaporate completely and leave no pollution behind
They are absorbed by the drains and disappear
They stay on the ground at the shopping centre forever
quiz.rationale: Rain runoff and blocked or open drains carry oil, detergent and litter from towns into rivers such as the Nairobi River, which is why the walk traced pollutant destinations.
quiz.placement: Predict: arrow sketch from the shopping centre to the river

quiz.prompt: During a pollution walk at a Kenyan shopping centre, learners see these items: plastic bottles, smoke from burning rubbish, hooting matatus, and soapy water from a car wash flowing into a drain. Which item is correctly matched to its type of pollution?
choices: Soapy water in a drain: solid waste pollution
Plastic bottles: air pollution
Smoke from burning rubbish: water pollution
Hooting matatus: noise pollution
quiz.rationale: Hooting is unwanted loud sound, so it is noise pollution. Plastic bottles are solid waste, smoke is air pollution and soapy water is water pollution.
quiz.placement: Observe: walk to the neighbouring shopping centre and observation table

quiz.prompt: A learner says, 'Only factories pollute rivers, so ordinary people in town do not cause river pollution.' Which observation from a shopping centre walk best shows that this idea is wrong?
choices: Factories release smoke into the air
Fish need oxygen to breathe
Some rivers are very long
Soapy water from car washes and litter flow into drains that lead to the river
quiz.rationale: Car wash detergent and litter from everyday activities enter drains and reach rivers, so ordinary people and small businesses also pollute.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher notes misconceptions such as 'only factories pollute'

quiz.prompt: In the Nairobi River, effluent and fertiliser runoff add nitrates and phosphates to the water. What is the first effect of these added nutrients?
choices: Fish grow faster because the water is clean
Algae and aquatic weeds grow much faster
Bacteria stop decomposing dead matter
The water gets more dissolved oxygen immediately
quiz.rationale: Nitrates and phosphates are nutrients that fertilise algae and weeds, causing an algal bloom (eutrophication). Low oxygen comes later.
quiz.placement: Explain: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning Final Explanation (nutrient input)

quiz.prompt: After an algal bloom, the algae die and sink. Why does the amount of dissolved oxygen in the river fall?
choices: Fish breathe out oxygen into the water
Bacteria decomposing the dead algae use up the oxygen
Nitrates change oxygen into carbon dioxide gas
Dead algae release large amounts of oxygen into the water
quiz.rationale: Decomposer bacteria respire aerobically while breaking down the dead algae and use up dissolved oxygen, leaving too little for fish.
quiz.placement: Explain: Reasoning part of the CER frame (bacterial decomposition and low oxygen)

quiz.prompt: The river water sometimes has an unpleasant smell. Which explanation is best supported by the Final Explanation?
choices: Nitrates and phosphates are gases with a bad smell
Decomposition without enough oxygen produces foul-smelling gases
Cold water always smells bad
Fish release a strong smell when they are happy
quiz.rationale: When oxygen is low, anaerobic decomposition of dead algae, weeds and fish produces foul-smelling gases.
quiz.placement: Explain: 'Which piece of evidence best supports your claim about the smell?'

quiz.prompt: Burning rubbish and fossil fuels in towns is linked to global warming. Which statement explains the link, and how it can affect fish in a river?
choices: Burning has no effect on the climate or on rivers
Burning makes more oxygen dissolve in river water, so fish suffocate
Burning removes carbon dioxide from the air, which cools rivers and kills fish
Burning releases greenhouse gases that warm the Earth, and warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen
quiz.rationale: Burning releases greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, which trap heat. Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, which stresses fish.
quiz.placement: Explain: linking burning waste and fossil fuels to greenhouse gases and climate change

quiz.prompt: A community wants to restore a polluted river where fish have disappeared. Which action matches the cause of the algal bloom best?
choices: Add more fish to the river without changing anything else
Plant trees on a hill far from the river
Hoot loudly near the river to chase away the algae
Reduce fertiliser and detergent use and treat effluent before it reaches the river
quiz.rationale: The bloom is caused by nitrates and phosphates from fertiliser, detergent and effluent, so cutting these inputs and treating effluent tackles the cause.
quiz.placement: Model: community solutions and poster to restore the river

quiz.prompt: In Lesson 1, a learner's model said that fish were disappearing because they were old or had no food. After the final model, which change in thinking shows the best use of evidence?
choices: Fish are lost because algae and weeds give them too much food
Fish are lost because the smell attracts predators
Fish are lost only because the river is too long
Fish are lost mainly because nutrient pollution leads to algal bloom, decomposition and low dissolved oxygen
quiz.rationale: The final model replaces the first ideas with the evidence-based chain: nutrient input, algal bloom, bacterial decomposition, low oxygen, fish loss and smell.
quiz.placement: Model: comparing the Lesson 1 model with the final model

quiz.prompt: Exit ticket: Why do fish decline when algae increase in a river?
choices: Dead algae are decomposed by bacteria that use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate or leave
Algae eat the fish directly
Algae add extra oxygen that is harmful to fish
Algae make the water too cold for fish
quiz.rationale: A large amount of dead algae feeds decomposing bacteria that use up dissolved oxygen, so fish cannot breathe and die or move away.
quiz.placement: Model: exit ticket question 2
